avoir-mal-vs-etre-malade.title: "J'ai mal à la tête" or "je suis malade"?
avoir-mal-vs-etre-malade.body: For pain in a specific part of the body, use avoir mal à: j'ai mal à la tête (I have a headache). For a general state of feeling unwell, without pointing to a specific part, use être malade: je suis malade (I'm sick). The choice of verb changes depending on whether you're describing a specific pain or a general state.

quest-ce-qui-ne-va-pas-ca-va-pas.title: "Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?" in everyday speech becomes "Ça va pas ?"
quest-ce-qui-ne-va-pas-ca-va-pas.body: The full question that opens the dialogue, Qu'est-ce qui ne va pas ?, tends to shrink a lot in everyday speech: Ça va pas ? (literally "it's not going well?") asks the same thing in a much shorter, more casual way — similar to "you OK?" in English.

trueFalse.claim: This sentence is used when someone has a headache.
trueFalse.whyNote: Correct — j'ai mal à la tête literally means "I have pain at the head", that is, a headache.
